questions.passage: São Paulo's economy has done well in Brazil's recent boom years, and it is still much bigger, but Rio's is growing faster, boosted by oil discoveries and winning its bid to host the 2016 Olympics. Last year Rio received $7.3 billion in foreign direct investment—seven times more than the year before and more than twice as much as São Paulo. Prime office rents in Rio are now higher than anywhere else in the Americas, north or south, according to Cushman and Wakefield, a property consultancy.
questions.question: According to the passage, in the past Sao Paulo's economy used to grow:
choices: At the same rate as Rio's economy
questions.explanation: The passage does not mention what the growth rate of both cities was in the past. It only mentions that recently Rio's economy has been growing faster. Therefore, (D) is the correct answer choice.

questions.passage: In 1804, the United States decided to fight the pirates of Barbary. Lieutenant Decatur and his small crew sailed into Tripoli harbour in order to attack them. Decatur's act, no matter how daring, did not alter radically the situation in the Mediterranean. Tripoli was defended by 25,000 soldiers and 115 cannons ashore, and 24 warships guarded the harbour. Against their enemy, Preble could pit only 1,060 men aboard seven ships, of which only the Constitution was heavy-gunned. Without troops to storm the port, all that Preble and his men could do was to disrupt the Pasha's economy by not allowing the pirates to practice their trade and to keep him on the defensive.
questions.question: How many of Preble's ships were not heavy-gunned?
questions.explanation: According to the text: " Against their enemy, Preble could pit only 1,060 men aboard seven ships, of which only the Constitution was heavy-gunned." Out of his seven ships, only one was heavy-gunned. Therefore, six of Preble's ships were not heavy-gunned.

questions.passage: Since the mid-1990s, about four men out of 10, and nearly a third of women population, have been overweight, and the proportion of people with normal weight has declined. Female obesity is inversely correlated with social class and income – obesity is highest among low income women in unskilled occupations – whereas socioeconomic factors make rather less difference to male weight.
questions.question: Females are more likely to be obese if they:
questions.explanation: According to the passage, "obesity is highest among low income women." (B) is incorrect since it notes that social class is inversely correlated with obesity – i.e. the higher the class, the less likely women are to be obese. Age and marital status are not mentioned in the passage at all.

questions.passage: Evidence shows that even if cosmic rays do affect the climate, the effect is very, very small. Changes in the number of cosmic rays hitting the atmosphere due to changes in solar activity cannot explain global warming. This is due to the fact that average cosmic ray intensities have been increasing since 1985, even as the world has warmed - the opposite of what should happen if cosmic rays produce climate-cooling clouds.
questions.question: Cosmic rays do not seriously affect the climate. This statement is:
questions.explanation: According to the text: "Evidence shows that even if cosmic rays do affect the climate, the effect is very, very small." Therefore, cosmic rays do not seriously affect the climate.

questions.passage: Venous Thromboembolism is a potentially lethal, yet common, blood clot disease which can be prevented. Out of those who survive it, almost a third experience long-term effects. Using data from 563 general practices in England and Wales, investigators studied more than 3.5 million patients aged 25 to 84 years with no previous history of blood clots. The rate of venous thromboembolism was around 15 cases per 10,000 person. The risk of venous thromboembolism in both men and women rises with increasing age, body mass index and quantity of cigarettes smoked each day.
questions.question: What did all studied patients share in common?
questions.explanation: According to the passage, the study included "more than 3.5 million patients... with no previous history of blood clots." As for the other answer choices, the passage mentions that "The risk in both men and women increased with increasing age, body mass index and quantity of cigarettes smoked each day" – so the study included both men and women (therefore, answer C can be eliminated), patients with varying BMI (A) and smokers (B).

questions.passage: Early results suggest that empathy and social functioning improve when a small area at the front of the brain is stimulated. However, concentration and the ability to communicate appear to be boosted when transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is used to suppress activity in a different region of the brain.
questions.question: Supression by TMS is applied in order to
questions.explanation: According to the passage, the "ability to communicate and concentration appear to be boosted when transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is used." Social functioning (Answer A) and empathy (Answer D) are improved when a different area of the brain is stimulated, and pain (B) is not mentioned at all in the passage.

questions.passage: Asians have several distinct family systems. To simplify: in South Asia it is traditional to have arranged, early marriages, in which men are dominant and the extended family is important. East Asia also has a male-dominated system, but one that stresses the nuclear family more; nowadays it has abandoned arranged marriages. In South-East Asia, women have somewhat more autonomy. But all three systems have escaped many of the social changes that have buffeted family life in the West since the 1960s.
questions.question: Which part of Asia has the least patriarchal family structure?
questions.explanation: According to the passage: "In South-East Asia, women have somewhat more autonomy" – that is, relative to the patriarchal structure of South and East Asia. Since South and East are answers (B) and (C), respectively, they can be eliminated. Answer (D), north-west, is not mentioned in the passage at all.

questions.passage: Until now, German economic growth has been the potential buffer for keeping the Eurozone system intact. But if the latest figures of a measly 0.1% growth for the second quarter of the year turn from a blip into a trend, two things will happen.The likelihood of a return to recession in Europe will increase, putting more pressure on the public finances of Greece, Portugal, Ireland, Italy, Spain and everybody else, and the reluctance of the German taxpayer to deliver rescue money in return for the continuance of the Euro might rise.
questions.question: What might be one of the consequences of low growth?
choices: Germany will stop functioning as an economic buffer.
Pressure will increase on Greece's public finances.
Rescue money will be transferred to countries in financial crisis.
questions.explanation: The passage refers to "a return to recession" and "putting more pressure on the public finances of Greece." Answers (A) and (C) are not mentioned in the passage at all, and (D) is incorrect since it states clearly that "the reluctance of the German taxpayer to deliver rescue money in return for the continuance of the Euro's assertability will intensify" – the opposite of answer (D).

questions.passage: The most important and continually emerging factor for financial firms to operate successfully in extended global markets is their ability to efficiently serve discerning, highly sophisticated, better educated, and more powerful consumers addicted to the ease and speed of technology. Financial firms that do not realize the importance of these customer-oriented traits are wasting their resources and will eventually perish. Businesses that fail to recognize the impact of these consumer-driven transformations will struggle to survive or cease to exist in a newly forged global financial service community that has been forever changed by deregulation.
questions.question: Companies should not perish if they recognize which of the following consumer traits?
questions.explanation:
Answer (B) is the correct answer because the text mentions that the consumer is "discerning," meaning he is perceptive.
Answer (A) is incorrect because the trait "efficiency" is mentioned in the text in relation to the company, not the consumer. Answer (C) is incorrect because the text does not mention anything about the consumer's financial situation. Answer (D) is incorrect because the text explicitly states the opposite—that the consumer is "better educated."

questions.passage: Scholars have come up with a long list of suspected causes, including rapacious invaders, a religious change of heart, and a shift to maritime trade that condemned an inland city. It's mostly guesswork: Roughly 1,300 inscriptions survive on temple doorjambs and freestanding stele, but the people of Angkor left not a single word explaining their kingdom's collapse.
questions.question: What have scholars tried to explain?
questions.explanation: According to the passage: "Scholars have come up with a long list of suspected causes" and "the people of Angkor left not a single word explaining their kingdom's collapse." Therefore, we can deduce that scholars tried to explain why the kingdom collapsed. Note you will need to read the entire passage in order to find the correct answer as these are the opening and closing sentences. Although all the other answer choices are mentioned in the passage, they are not what the scholars are trying to explain – rather the factors they studied when trying to explain why the kingdom collapsed.

questions.passage:
In the year 730 B.C., a man by the name of Piye decided the only way to save Egypt from itself was to invade it. Things would get bloody before salvation came.
Piye's soldiers sailed north up the Nile River. At Thebes, the capital of Upper Egypt, they disembarked. Believing there was a proper way to wage holy wars, Piye instructed his soldiers to purify themselves before combat by bathing in the Nile, dressing themselves in fine linen, and sprinkling their bodies with water from the temple at Karnak, a site holy to the ram-headed sun god Amun. Piye himself feasted and offered sacrifices to Amun. Thus sanctified, the commander and his men commenced to do battle with every army in their path.
questions.question: How many steps did Piye's soldiers take to ready themselves for war?
questions.explanation: The passage lists three steps in which Piye instructed his soldiers to prepare themselves: "Piye instructed his soldiers to purify themselves before combat by bathing in the Nile (1), dressing themselves in fine linen (2), and sprinkling their bodies with water from the temple at Karnak (3)." It also states that Piye himself "feasted and offered sacrifices to Amun" – but that is not something his soldiers did, so we are left with the three steps the soldiers were told to take to prepare for war.

questions.passage: Jack Mellor at the University of Bristol, UK, exposed slices of rats' hippocampi to the low-oxygen conditions typical of a stroke. Neurons in the hippocampi known to resist stroke damage acted differently from a population of vulnerable cells: they removed receptors for the neurotransmitter glutamate from their cell surface, reducing their sensitivity to the chemical. Glutamate floods the brain during a stroke.
questions.question: Vulnerable cells during a stroke:
questions.explanation: This question requires some inference. According to the passage, "Neurons in the hippocampi known to resist stroke damage... removed receptors for the neurotransmitter glutamate." From this, we can infer that neurons that are vulnerable are receptive to glutamate. So answer (C) is the best answer. Note that answers (A) and (B) refer to cells that resist stroke, so they cannot be the correct answer. Answer (D) is not mentioned in the passage at all.

questions.passage: Around 650,000 Europeans die annually from strokes, triggered when the blood supply to a part of the brain is blocked or severely reduced. A Belgian research institute is helping develop an innovative new photonic chip to prevent stroke death in an EU-funded research partnership made possible by the Enterprise Europe Network. With €2.6 million in funding, the consortium is developing a technology that would enable doctors to diagnose and treat stroke early at point of care – instead of waiting for the standard battery of medical tests whose results often come too late.
questions.question: How can the new invention help doctors and patients?
questions.explanation: The passage states that the new invention is a "technology that would enable doctors to diagnose and treat stroke early" – that is, answer (B). Answers (A) and (C) are not mentioned in the passage at all, and as for answer (D) – note that the passage mentions that the new invention is not meant to prevent strokes, but "to prevent stroke death."

questions.passage: To fight the Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacterium, the scientists used a strain of the E.coli bacteria that is normally present in the human gut. They inserted into E.coli foreign DNA fragments that empowered it to sense the offending pathogen and quickly produce and release a deadly toxin. Once it (re-engineered E.coli) detects the presence of the aeruginosa, it produces a toxin and the killing molecule will be released to kill the pathogen.
questions.question: Why did scientists use foreign DNA fragments?
questions.explanation: According to the passage: "Once it [re-engineered E.coli] detects the presence of the aeruginosa, it produces a toxin and the killing molecule will be released." Answer (A) is incorrect as entering the human gut is not mentioned as a problem. (B) is incorrect as the scientists used E. Coli to kill the Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacterium, and (D) is incorrect since the E. Coli produced a molecule, not bacteria.

questions.passage:
One day, there may be more than X-ray machines and full-body scanners awaiting you at the airport.
During their 4-hour shifts in the detector, the mice mill about in a common area in each cartridge as air is passed over people paused in the archway and through the cartridge. When the mice sniff traces of any of eight key explosives in the air, they are conditioned to avoid the scent and flee to a side chamber, triggering an alarm. To avoid false positives, more than one mouse must enter the room at the same time.
questions.question: When might a false alarm occur?
choices: When a mouse flees to a side chamber
When all the mice stay in the common area
When several mice flee to the side chamber while explosives are absent
questions.explanation:
The alarm is triggered whenever several mice flee to the side chamber. So, if they go to the side chamber while explosives are absent, the alarm will be triggered falsely.
Answer (A) is incorrect because the alarm will not be triggered if only one mouse flees to the side chamber.
Answer (B) is incorrect because the alarm will not trigger if all the mice stay in the common area.
Answer (C) is incorrect because if the mice only smell the explosives but do not flee, the alarm will not go off at all. This answer does not mention what the mice do after smelling the explosives.

questions.passage: In January the first crowds gathered to demand reform, barricades went up and within hours the news was transmitted to millions. Encouraged by what they saw and heard crowds turned out in cities thousands of miles apart to demand votes, jobs, constitutions and their human rights. Governments were caught paralyzed and watched helplessly as troops refused to fire on crowds. Ministers fell and kings fled. The year was 1848, and if you think 2011 has been turbulent, it has a long way to go before it matches the seismic events of 1848, the Year of Revolutions.
questions.question: In comparison with 1848, events in 2011 were:
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states that "if you think 2011 has been turbulent, it has a long way to go before it matches the seismic events of 1848" – so events of 2011 were less severe.

questions.passage: There are three basic sources of productivity: labor, management, and technology. Construction projects present the construction manager with many challenges. Among them is the coordination of material, equipment, finances, and labor that must come together to produce the desired output. The analysis of any construction project will show that the construction manager is seeking to manage resources effectively and efficiently in order to complete the project. Those managers that seek to understand human behavior and apply the principles of motivation theory to motivate the construction worker can benefit through improved productivity.
questions.question: How can the labor productivity source be enhanced?
questions.explanation:
According to the passage, "managers that seek to understand human behaviour and apply the principles of motivation... can benefit through improved productivity."

(A) and (D), are not mentioned in the passage at all. (B) is mentioned as the common practice – not as an enhancement of productivity.

questions.passage: The Chinese central state regulators have marketed the fuel tax as having the following energy efficiency benefits: inducing pro-environment behaviors from vehicle owners and carmakers, promoting public transportation, and alleviating China's dependency on imported crude over the long run. State officials have also claimed that the fuel tax will save vehicle owners significant amounts of money by eliminating numerous and proliferating local fees. Aside from a dearth of domestic scientific studies to predict the policy effects, these official claims actually detract from the important issues at stake.
questions.question: What advantage did State officials add that was not mentioned by state regulators?
questions.explanation: According to the passage: "State officials have also claimed that the fuel tax will save vehicle owners significant money." The phrase "have also claimed" serves as a clue that this is not part of the official regulations. (B) and (C) are mentioned as benefits the state regulators have mentioned, while (D), although mentioned in the passage, is not an advantage at all.

questions.passage: To have a normal retirement age under the age of 65, your employer must be able to justify the age objectively. This means that age is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim. In the case of retirement, your employer may be able to show that, for example, the lower age is needed for health and safety requirements that cannot be achieved in any other way. However, it will be difficult for an employer to justify a retirement age below 65.
questions.question: What might serve as a cause for retiring an employee?
questions.explanation: According to the passage: "In the case of retirement, your employer may be able to show that, for example, a lower age is needed for health and safety requirements." The other choices are not mentioned in the passage.

questions.passage: We stake our civilizations on the coasts and mighty rivers. Our deepest dread is the threat of having too little moisture—or too much. We've lately raised the Earth's average temperature by 0.74°C (1.3°F), a number that sounds inconsequential. But these words do not: flood, drought, hurricane, rising sea levels, bursting levees. Water is the visible face of climate and, therefore, climate change. Shifting rain patterns flood some regions and dry up others as nature demonstrates a grave physics lesson: Hot air holds more water molecules than cold.
questions.question: What is not mentioned as related to Changes in water patterns:
questions.explanation: In the passage we can find mention of temperature changes (D): "We've lately raised the Earth's average temperature," and climatic changes (A), hurricanes, (C): "flood, drought, hurricane, rising sea levels, bursting levees. Water is the visible face of climate and, therefore, climate change." The only answer not mentioned is changes in the ozone layer – (B).

questions.passage: The Macondo incident, in which a subsea oil well exploded in the Mexican Gulf, was unprecedented, but so was the oil industry's response. Based on the work of various industry task forces, improvements have been made in prevention, capping and containment, and spill response. Task force recommendations are driving improvement in standards and practices related to well design and installation, and the industry now has the capability to quickly contain and cap a well in very deep water.
questions.question: What capability was upgraded after the explosion?
choices: Installing wells in very deep water
questions.explanation:
The passage clearly states that "the industry now has the capability to quickly contain and cap..."
Answer A is incorrect as there is no mention of installing wells in very deep water.
Answer B is incorrect as the question asks about capability, rather than improvements in standards and practices
Answer C is incorrect as the passage notes that a task force submitted recommendations for improvements, not for the recruitment of task forces.

questions.passage: The government's efforts at repressing production in Laos were augmented happily by a simultaneous explosion in poppy growth in Afghanistan. The Taliban had seized Kabul in 1996 but it wasn't until 2000 that Afghanistan's opium producers really hit their stride. That year Afghanistan's market overtook Myanmar as the world's largest and began dictating prices worldwide (to ignore the remarkable blip of 2001). By 2006 it was growing seven times the amount of Myanmar, Thailand and Laos combined. A subsequent glut sent global prices plummeting, aiding the eradication efforts of the South-East Asian governments.
questions.question: During the past millennium, the opium market was dominated by:
questions.explanation:
"The Taliban had seized Kabul in 1996 but it wasn't until 2000 that Afghanistan's opium producers really hit their stride. That year Afghanistan's market overtook Myanmar as the world's largest...".

We can learn that Myanmar dominated the market before 2000, during the past millennium.

questions.passage: A GHG tax can be levied at any point in the energy supply chain. Most proposals target upstream suppliers of coal, oil, and natural gas as opposed to midstream points (electric utilities or oil refineries) and downstream (energy-using industries, households). Measuring the carbon content of fuels is a straightforward task and there are relatively fewer fuel producers and importers. To be fully inclusive, a downstream tax would have to fall on millions of users, increasing the likelihood that the program's scope would be more limited with higher aggregate and administrative costs.
questions.question: Why not tax downstream users?
questions.explanation: The passage states that "a downstream tax... would be more limited with higher aggregate and administrative costs."

questions.passage: Herod was born in 73 B.C. and grew up in Judaea. The Hasmonaean monarchy that had ruled Judaea for 70 years was split by a vicious fight for the throne between two princely brothers, Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II. The kingdom was in turn caught in a larger geopolitical struggle between the Roman legions to the north and west, and the Parthians, historic enemies of Rome, to the east. Herod's father, the chief adviser to Hyrcanus and a gifted general, threw in his lot with the Romans, who banished Aristobulus and made Hyrcanus king of Judaea.
questions.question: Herod's father:
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states that "Herod's father... threw in his lot with the Romans, who banished Aristobulus and made Hyrcanus king" – from this we can deduce that he supported Hyrcanus.

questions.passage: New DNA analysis of clay-bound pills from a Roman shipwreck confirms traces of the same dried plants (including carrot, radish, cabbage, celery, wild onion, and parsley) described in ancient Greek medical texts. The brownish, coin-size pills—preserved in tin boxes for two millennia—are the first proof that the writings were "not just theoretical but actually applied."
questions.question: 2000 years ago some dried plants:
questions.explanation: The passage states that DNA analysis "confirms traces of the same dried plants" – that is, they were found then. (A) is incorrect as obviously the plants were found, so were not only written about. (C) is incorrect since the plants look today like coin-size pills, but we have no knowledge of what they looked like 2,000 years ago. (D) is not mentioned in the passage at all so we cannot tell if they were eaten or not.

questions.passage: Drinking enough water can improve memory capabilities and aid coping with fatigue during the afternoon. It can reduce constipation when consumed in addition to grapes and cranberries. According to one method used to induce drinking more water, a person receives a point each time water is substituted for coffee or alcohol. Along with each point, a predetermined sum of money is put aside. When the score reaches 20 points, the money is used for a reward. Finally, although adequate drinking of water hasn't been shown to directly cause a weight decrease, it has been linked to weight loss.
questions.question: What do grapes and cranberries assist in?
questions.explanation: The passage states that drinking water "can reduce constipation when consumed in addition to grapes and cranberries"; so consuming these fruits helps with reducing constipation. Answer (B) is incorrect as grapes and cranberries are not mentioned in this context (although water is). Saving money is not mentioned in the passage at all – although one method of encouraging drinking water involves money. Answer (D) is also not mentioned in the context of grapes and cranberries.

questions.passage: Among students preparing for final exams, some rely only on the technique of short, frequent study sessions to improve studying results, and others observe only the natural learning sequence of moving from general issues to specific issues, also known as "top-down" learning. Those who rely only on the natural learning sequence get higher final exam scores than do those who rely only on short, frequent study sessions. The natural learning sequence is therefore more effective than short, frequent study sessions in helping students improve their final exam scores.
questions.question: What is said on natural learning technique?
questions.explanation: According to the passage, "the natural learning sequence [is] of moving from general issues to specific issues, also known as "top-down" learning", as Answer (B) states. (A) and (C) are not mentioned in this context at all. As for answer (D) – the passage mentions that this technique is MORE effective, not less.

questions.passage: The World Meteorological Organization announced its finding last week that global mean temperatures for 2010 were 0.53°C above the 1961-1990 mean, 0.01°C warmer than 2005 and 0.02°C above 1998. With the comparison having a margin of uncertainty of 0.09°C, the three years are considered tied for the hottest year on record. That followed results the previous week from NOAA, which found 2010 and 2005 tied as the hottest years ever, and NASA, which found the same thing. (They both think 1998 was a bit colder).
questions.question: According to NASA, the hottest years ever were:
questions.explanation: The World Meteorological Organization, NOAA and NASA all agree that 2010 and 2005 were the hottest years ever. They disagree regarding 1998, which NOAA and NAA think were a bit colder than the World Meteorological Organization's assessment. That makes 2005 and 2010 the two hottest years, according to the passage.

questions.passage: When an insect brushes against a hair on the leaf of a Venus flytrap, the bending triggers a tiny electric charge. The charge builds up inside the tissue of the leaf but is not enough to stimulate the snap, which keeps the Venus flytrap from reacting to false alarms like raindrops. A moving insect, however, is likely to brush a second hair, adding enough charge to trigger the leaf to close.
questions.question: To catch its prey, A Venus flytrap uses:
questions.explanation: According to the passage, an insect touching a hair on the flytrap will trigger an electric charge. A second touch will add enough charge to close the leaf. Poison, water and stickiness – answers (A), (B) and (D) – are not mentioned in the passage at all.

questions.passage: Asian markets joined the expansion movement in 1996 when financial reforms brought about deregulation in Japan. Relatively far-reaching financial systems in that country became competitive in a changing global environment. By 1999, nearly all remaining restrictions on foreign exchange transactions between Japan and other countries were lifted. Following the changes in the Asian financial market, the U.S. continued to implement several additional stages of deregulation, concluding with the GLB Act of 1999, which allowed for the consolidation of major financial players, pushing U.S.-domiciled financial service companies to a total of $221 billion in 2000.
questions.question: Lifting monetary restrictions allowed Japan to transact with which countries?
questions.explanation: The passage mentions that "restrictions on foreign exchange transactions between Japan and other countries were lifted" – i.e. Japan was now able to interact with all countries. Answer (B) is incorrect as the US is mentioned in connection with deregulation on its side. Asian and European countries, answers (C) and (D), are not mentioned in the passage at all.

questions.passage: After rising very slowly for millennia, the number of humans on Earth was just starting to take off. A century and a half later, when another scientist reported the discovery of human egg cells, the world's population had doubled to more than a billion. A century after that, around 1930, it had doubled again to two billion. The acceleration since then has been astounding.
questions.question: What was the world's population around 1830?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (C).

According to the passage: "A century after that, around 1930, it had doubled again to two billion." So a century before, in 1830, the number of people on Earth was half of that – one billion.

questions.passage: In July, Chinese media reported that the Hong-Kong-based foundation called “Asia Pacific Exchange and Co-operation Foundation”, which is widely thought to have China's backing, had signed an agreement with UNIDO, the UN's industrial-development organization, to invest $3 billion in Lumbini, a village in southern Nepal. Lumbini is the birthplace of the Buddha, which the project aimed to make a “Mecca for Buddhists”; with train links, an international airport, hotels and a Buddhist university.
questions.question: “Mecca for Buddhists” would be founded in
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (D).

The passage mentions "Lumbini, a village in southern Nepal. Lumbini is the birthplace of the Buddha, which the project planned to make a 'Mecca for Buddhists'" – so the "Mecca" would be built in Nepal.

questions.passage: A coronary stent is a metal tube placed in the coronary arteries, to keep them open in the treatment of coronary heart disease. The cardiologist uses a projectional radiographer to assess the location and estimate the size of the blockage by injecting a contrast medium through the guide catheter and viewing the flow of blood through the downstream coronary arteries. Intravascular ultrasound may be used to assess the lesion's thickness and hardness. The cardiologist uses this information to decide whether to treat the lesion with a stent.
questions.question: How many electrical medical instruments may be used by the cardiologist?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (B).

Notice the question refers to electrical Instruments: "The cardiologist uses a projectional radiographer to assess the location and estimate the size of the blockage by injecting a contrast medium through the guide catheter and viewing the flow of blood through the downstream coronary arteries. Intravascular ultrasound may be used to assess the lesion's thickness and hardness." – that is, TWO electrical instruments.

questions.passage: The key problem in running a paternity test on a pregnant woman's blood is working out which DNA comes from the fetus and the woman. The new test establishes the mother's SNP profile by separating blood cells, the vast majority of which will come from the woman, from the clear plasma. Algorithms then "subtract" the maternal profile from that recorded from DNA in the blood plasma – around 10 percent of which can come from fetal cells that have broken down – to produce a fetal profile for comparison against DNA samples from the possible fathers.
questions.question: Why is it difficult to perform a paternity test on an embryo?
choices: The fetus's DNA is not yet determined
It has not been put to test yet
We cannot tell the DNA's origin
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (D).

According to the passage: "The key problem in running a paternity test on a pregnant woman's blood is working out which DNA comes from the fetus."

questions.passage: Using heat—in the form of steam—to liberate disobligingly thick and gunky oil, which would otherwise stay in the ground, is nothing new. GlassPoint, a small Californian company, thinks it can make steam for oil recovery more cleanly and cheaply by using sunshine to do the heating. GlassPoint's boss thinks that taking capital costs and the lifetime of the plant into account his firm can produce steam at $3.78 per million British thermal units (btu), which is $3.58 a gigajoule. Steam from gas comes in at $5.79 per million btu. A pilot project in California, he says, has been producing steam as intended since the beginning of the year.
questions.question: Using solar power instead of gas to produce steam would cost:
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (A).

To find the percentage difference in cost between producing steam using solar power versus gas, follow these steps:
1. Identify the costs of producing steam:
Using solar power: $3.78 per million BTU
Using gas: $5.79 per million BTU
2. Calculate the difference in cost:
Difference=5.79−3.78=2.01
3. Calculate the ratio between the difference and the cost of using gas:
2.01/ 5.79 = 0.347
4. Find the percentage by multiplying the ratio by 100:
0.347 X 100 = 34.7 %
Therefore, using solar power instead of gas to produce steam would cost 34.7% less, which is about 35%.

questions.passage: There's little wonder Russians are toasting oil: These are boom times. Global oil prices have increased tenfold since 1998, and Russia has pulled ahead of Saudi Arabia as the world's top crude oil producer. The Kremlin's budget now overflows with funds for new schools, roads, and national defense projects, and Moscow's nouveau riche are plunking down millions of dollars for mansion-scale "dachas."
questions.question: The Russians now produce crude oil because:
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (C).

According to the passage: "There's little wonder Russians are toasting oil: These are boom times. Global oil prices have increased tenfold since 1998." Russia has been producing oil as the prices rise.

questions.passage: The Germans learned lessons from the Somme and other battles. They moved away from defending linear trenches to a much looser and more flexible system of defending strongpoints and using reserves in the counterattack role. They abandoned their policy of automatically counterattacking every Allied gain. But ultimately they learned a wrong lesson. By concentrating resources on a relatively small number of elite “storm” units, they reduced the overall quality of their army. In the long run this proved to be a disastrous policy.
questions.question: How many lessons were learned?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (C).

The passage mentions three lessons: "They moved away from defending linear trenches to a much looser and more flexible system of defending strongpoints and using reserves in the counterattack role [lesson 1]. They abandoned their policy of automatically counterattacking every Allied gain [lesson 2]. But ultimately they learned a wrong lesson. By concentrating resources on a relatively small number of elite “storm” units" [lesson 3]. Note the first lesson includes several parts but they all come down to changing the defence of their trenches. Note, also, that the third lesson was wrong.

questions.passage: Mars has long exerted a pull on the human imagination.The erratically moving red star in the sky was seen as sinister or violent by the ancients: The Greeks identified it with Ares, the god of war; the Babylonians named it after Nergal, god of the underworld. To the ancient Chinese, it was Ying-huo, the fire planet. Even after Copernicus proposed, in 1543, that the sun and not the Earth was the center of the local cosmos, the eccentricity of Mars's celestial motions continued as a puzzle until, in 1609, Johannes Kepler analyzed all the planetary orbits as ellipses, with the sun at one focus.
questions.question: Who lived in the 17th century?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (A).

The passage mentions that "in 1609, Johannes Kepler analysed all the planetary orbits as ellipses" – so Kepler lived and operated in the 17th century.
Note that the 17th century refers to the years from 1601 to 1700, and that's why 1609 falls within the 17th century. This happens because the way we count centuries starts with the year 1 AD. The first century (1st century) covered the years 1 to 100 AD. So:
• The 1st century is from 1 to 100.
• The 2nd century is from 101 to 200.
• And so on.

questions.passage: South Africa's economy has shown modest recovery in early 2010. It is expected to register GDP growth rates between 3 and 4 percent between 2011 and 2014. The sectors that are likely to grow the most are the manufacturing, finance, real estate and business services sectors. The economy will be shored up by the strengthening of the local manufacturing sector, due to the government's commitment to development. It will also be bolstered by the relatively high levels of foreign direct investment that has stimulated the finance, real estate and business services sectors.
questions.question: Government commitment to development will cause which of the following?
choices: Strengthening of the local manufacturing sector
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (B).

According to the passage: "The economy will be shored up by the strengthening of the local manufacturing sector, as part of the government's commitment to development."

questions.passage: Some 40,000 people have been killed so far in Mexico's heightened drug war, which is nearing five years old. In spite of the violence, Mexico's economy has been doing reasonably well. Though the border with the United States has seen the worst of the fighting, trade between the two countries is at an all-time high. Crucial to keeping the investment and visitors flowing is the fact that the violence has been highly concentrated, and that most of the victims, we are told are people who are themselves involved in organized crime.
questions.question: High trade between Mexico and USA is contradictory to
questions.explanation: "Though the border with the United States has seen the worst of the fighting, trade between the two countries is at an all-time high."

questions.passage: Admittedly, absolute numbers of committed forces per nation in NATO are seen by some as presenting an unfair comparison. Some analysts say that percentages of population and the gross domestic product are a far better assessment. If the fact that the world's largest collective GDP can't handle the task is not enough, let's take a look at the nations involved. French defense budget is 1.8 percent of GDP, the British is 2.2 percent, the U.S. is 4 percent, a lot more than the 1.2 percent of Germany."
questions.question: Which country has the highest defense budget, as percent of its GDP?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (D).

We can see the passage mentions that: "[the] French defense budget is 1.8 percent of GDP, the British is 2.2 percent, the U.S. is 4 percent, much more than Germany's 1.2 percent. Out of all the countries mentioned in the answers, the U.S has the highest budget as a percentage of its GDP – 4% – compared to 1.2%-2.2% in the other countries.

questions.passage: Although Britain would not use African troops in Europe, as this would "undermine the dignity of the white man", to Britain's horror and disapproval, France used some 160,000 Africans from its west African colonies in Europe, with another 65,000 used elsewhere. Britain used some 50,000 African troops and about one million 'carriers' in the African campaigns and some 1,000 were used in Mesopotamia. The death rates were high: in the east African campaigns, over 11,000 African soldiers and around 100,000 carriers died; some 22,000 were wounded and/or missing-in-action.
questions.question: As opposed to Britain, where did France use African soldiers?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (A).

According to the passage, "Although Britain would not use African troops in Europe... France sent some 160,000 Africans from its West African colonies to Europe" – so Britain did not employ African troops in Europe, while France did. The passage also states that Britain did use African soldiers in Africa and Mesopotamia, so answers (B) and (C) are incorrect. As for answer (D), India is not mentioned in the passage at all.

questions.passage: It was Soviet engineer Sergei Korolev whose rockets took the first craft into space, the first animal into space and the first man into space. He was also behind the initial probe landing on the moon and the original photographic glimpse of its mysterious dark side. German born Von Braun was the genius behind the American space program that for many years lived in the shadow of the Soviets before achieving the ultimate triumph when his Saturn 5 rocket propelled Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins towards the moon in 1969.
questions.question: The invention of whom sent astronauts to the moon?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (D).

According to the passage, "[the] German-born Von Braun was the genius behind the American space program," and "his Saturn 5 rocket propelled Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins towards the moon."

questions.passage: Both human liver enzymes and bacteria can process caffeine and other drugs. Liver enzymes can remove the CH₃ groups stuck to the rings, just as bacterial enzymes do, resulting in caffeine derivatives, the most simple of which is known as xanthine, the door. The bacteria hang onto them, chopping down the rings to their component elements and harvesting energy.
questions.question: In bacteria, caffeine
choices: is not processed in the liver
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (A).

The passage mentions that "bacteria hang onto them, chopping down the rings to their component elements and harvesting energy" – so caffeine can be used for creating energy in bacteria.

questions.passage: BMAA is a compound that is produced by cyanobacteria, the blue-green algae that live in soil, lakes, and oceans. Cyanobacteria are consumed by fish and other aquatic creatures. Recent studies have found BMAA in seafood, suggesting that certain diets and locations may put people at particular risk. More worrisome, blooms of cyanobacteria are becoming increasingly common, fueling fears that their toxic by-product may be quietly fomenting an upsurge in ALS—and possibly other neurological disorders like Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's as well.
questions.question: What kinds of hazards reside in sea food?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (D).

The answer to this question can be found in several places in the passage. First, the passage says that "BMAA is a compound that is produced by cyanobacteria." Then, it explains that this compound is dangerous: "recent studies have found BMAA in seafood, suggesting that certain diets and locations may put people at particular risk." The final sentence mentions why not only BMAA but also cyanobacteria themselves are dangerous: "More worrisome, blooms of cyanobacteria are becoming increasingly common." Combining all these gives you the answer that both cyanobacteria and BMAA are dangerous, and since BMAA is a product of cyanobacteria, if the first is found in sea food, so is the second.

questions.passage: A new study found a strong relationship between the highest measured sea levels and the incidence of coastal floods, and highlights the most vulnerable areas to coastal flooding, which include parts of Portsmouth, Southampton, Hayling Island, Fareham and Cowes. The most severe flood in the data set resulted from the storm surge events of 13-17 December 1989 when eight consecutive extreme high waters occurred. The study, which is published online in the Natural Hazards journal, suggests that while extreme sea-level events are becoming more common, the occurrence of flood events is not increasing.
questions.question: How many extreme sea level events must occur to surpass the current record?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (A).

According to the passage, "The most severe flood in the dataset resulted from the storm surge events of 13-17 December 1989 when eight consecutive extremely high waters occurred." So in order to surpass that, nine floods must occur.

questions.passage: El Niño tends to bring hotter, drier conditions - and La Niña cooler ones - to tropical countries, but both have less of an influence on temperate countries. A climate analysis included 175 countries and 234 conflicts, over half of which caused more than 1000 deaths. It found that the risk of conflict in tropical countries rose from 3 per cent during La Niña years to 6 per cent during El Niño years. The effect was absent from countries only weakly affected by these climate cycles.
questions.question: What correlates with cooler climatic conditions?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (A).

The passage states that La Niña brings cooler climate conditions, and that "[the] risk of conflict in tropical countries rose by 3 per cent during La Niña years" – so a risk of 3% correlates with cooler years.

questions.passage: No matter where they come from, from the Alps to the Andes, all self-respecting rock climbers yearn to make a pilgrimage to "the valley" to measure themselves against its giants: El Capitan, a shimmering prow of stone so immense it makes the hundred-foot ponderosa pines at its base look miniature; Cathedral Rocks, a dark fortress forever in the shade; and Half Dome, a granite apple cleaved in half, its soaring northwest face an invitation to the boldest climbers in the world. To climb here is a rite of passage.
questions.question: The text compares climbing El Capitan and Half Dome to
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (C).

According to the passage: "To climb here is a rite of passage" – a comparison with undergoing the ceremony of becoming an adult.

questions.passage: Tibetan Buddhism has a religious hierarchy with the Dalai Lama at the top, followed by the Panchen Lama. The Dalai Lama is traditionally involved in recognizing the Panchen Lama, and the Panchen Lama is part of the process by which each new Dalai Lama is chosen. China has its eyes on a complex struggle that will play out after the death of the current 76-year-old Dalai Lama, who lives in exile in India.
questions.question: What is not true about Tibetian Buddhism?
choices: Panchen Lama is second in hierarchy
Dalai Lama is first in hierarchy
Panchen Lama influences the choice of a new Dalai Lama
The Dalai Lama lives in Tibet
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (D).

The passage mentions "the current 76-year-old Dalai Lama, who lives in exile in India."

questions.passage: Recruiters spend their time building relations with prospective employees or people who could refer them to talent. Social media in general has increased the ability to build and maintain relations with people. Since social media has proved to accelerate relationships and knowledge of these relationships, that information can be put to better use to support all of human resources needs. Social tools can be used to manage compensation, benefits, acquiring talent, grooming talent, aligning employee success with business success, matching like-minded employees and cultivating innovation within the organization.
questions.question: How can social media tools be employed at HR departments?
choices: Compensate workers in case of loss of competencies
Developing innovative applications for social networks
Recruiters can be referred to potential talents
Further investigate people's private life for matching
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (C).

According to the passage: "Recruiters spend their time building relations with prospective employees or people who could refer them to talent. Social media in general have increased the ability to build and maintain relations with people." So social media can assist in the task of referring new talent. Answer (A) is incorrect. Although compensation is mentioned in the passage, it does not say anything about loss of competencies. (B) and (D) are not mentioned in the passage at all.

questions.passage: The Patent Cooperation Treaty provides a unified procedure for filing patent applications to protect inventions in each of its contracting states. A single filing of an international application is made with a Receiving Office in one language. It then results in a search performed by an International Searching Authority, as well as in a written opinion regarding the patentability of the invention, which is the subject of the application. It is followed by a preliminary examination. Finally, the relevant national or regional authorities administer matters related to the examination of application and issuance of patent.
questions.question: What is the maximal number of steps required from application to issuance, inclusive?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (B).

Here are the steps mentioned in the passage: "A single filing of an international application is made with a Receiving Office in one language [Step 1]. It then results in a search performed by an International Searching Authority [step 2], accompanied by a written opinion regarding the patentability of the invention, which is the subject of the application [step 3]. It is followed by a preliminary examination [step 4]. Finally, the relevant national or regional authorities administer matters related to the examination of application and issuance of patent [step 5]."

questions.passage: War and politics visibly intertwined with music in the 20th century, under totalitarianism and after it. Classical music blared constantly in the choreographed background to Nazi life. For a time, the classical repertoire was deemed to have lost its moral stature because of the Nazis' embrace. This was one reason why some composers tried to scrap classical forms and explore the alternatives, leading to the dissonant pandemonium of experimental music in the 1950s., A left-wing sociologist and musician wrote in 1949 that preserving tonality betrayed a fascist mentality.
questions.question: During the 20th century classical music:
choices: Was not embraced by the Nazis
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (B).

According to the passage, "the classical repertoire was deemed to have lost its moral stature because of the Nazis' embrace. This was one reason why some composers tried to scrap classical forms and explore the alternatives, leading to the dissonant pandemonium of experimental music in the 1950s." Since the classical repertoire was embraced by the Nazis, a change was sought by some composers.

questions.passage: Greece – the first EU country of entry for many thousands of asylum-seekers does not have – and has not had for several years – asylum-determination procedures or adequate reception conditions in line with international law. It has also not ensured that such asylum-seekers are treated with respect for their dignity on arrival. Many of those seeking international protection have been detained in horrendous conditions, then released and left to live destitute on the streets. Some have been removed from Greece despite the fact that such removal placed them at real risk of further grave human rights violations.
questions.question: What did Greece's inadequate policies prevent from people on their arrival?
questions.explanation: Many of those seeking international protection have been detained in horrendous conditions, then released and left to live destitute on the streets. Some have been removed from Greece despite the fact that such removal placed them at real risk of further grave human rights violations.

questions.passage: Shinto is a religion in which devotees are concerned with their local shrine rather than the religion as a whole, having a tiny shrine-altar at home. Because it is focused on the land of Japan, Shinto is clearly an ethnic religion. Therefore, Shinto is little interested in missionary work, and rarely practiced outside its country of origin. It is also an unofficial national religion with shrines that draw visitors from across the country. Because ritual rather than belief is at the heart of Shinto, Japanese people don't usually think of Shinto as a religion.
questions.question: What makes Shinto become local and not globally spread?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (D).

This quote from the passage explains that Shinto is an ethnic religion that is rarely practised outside Japan: "Because it is focused on the land of Japan Shinto is clearly an ethnic religion. Therefore, Shinto is little interested in missionary work, and is rarely practised outside its country of origin." Answer (A), missionary work, is incorrect as it is the opposite of what the passage says, and answers (B) and (C) are characteristics of Shinto, but are unrelated to practising Shinto globally.

questions.passage: Applications for patents in the UK should be filed at the Patent Office in London or Newport. It is possible for anyone to apply for a patent by supplying a description of the invention, but professional advice should always be sought when possible, particularly if filing a complicated patent application. The extra expenditure involved in using a patent attorney is almost essential, mainly because the protection obtained depends on the wording used to describe the invention. The initial application can be a description accompanied by drawings.
questions.question: What is a recommended action for non-trivial patent applications?
choices: Perform the filing in London only
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (C).

As the passage states: "professional advice should always be sought where possible, particularly if filing a complicated patent application. The extra expenditure involved in using a patent attorney is almost essential." So if the patent is not trivial, it is best to hire the professional help of a patent attorney. Note that answers (A) and (B), patent description and drawing, are part of the initial application of any patent and are not specific to non-trivial patents, and that answer (D) is incorrect, as the passage clearly states that all applications can be made either in Newport or in London.

questions.passage: Being happy and staying happy is not a direct result of your genetic makeup or life circumstances only, people can add to their capacity for happiness through techniques that can be learned. The much-discussed "happiness set point" that is more genetically determined, accounts for about half of someone's happiness and 10% can be attributed to life situations.
questions.question: What percentage of happiness capacity can be learned through techniques?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (A).

For this question, you need to calculate how much various factors contribute to happiness. According to the passage: "[the] happiness set point," which is more genetically determined, accounts for about half of someone's happiness, while 10% can be attributed to life situations." So 50% is the genetic set-point and 10% more are life situations. That leaves us with 40% of happiness that can be learned through techniques.

questions.passage: In 1948 the Bell Telephone Laboratories announced the invention of a tiny electronic semiconductor, “an amazingly simple device” that could do anything a vacuum tube could do and more efficiently. It was a crystalline sliver, so small that 100 would fit in the palm of a hand. “It may have far-reaching significance in electronics and electrical communication,” Bell Labs declared in a press release, and for once the reality surpassed the hype. The transistor sparked the revolution in electronics, setting the technology on its path of miniaturization.
questions.question: The transistor was:
choices: As small as a human hand
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (C).

According to the passage: "the reality surpassed the hype. The transistor sparked the revolution in electronics." So expectations from the transistor were much exceeded. It was obviously not a disappointment, so answer (A) is incorrect. It wasn't the size of a hand (answer B), but actually much smaller, and it wasn't invented in the 19th century (D); it was invented in 1948, which is the 20th century.

questions.passage: Germany's GDP grew at a mere 0.1% in the second quarter of 2011, compared with 1.3% in the first. The national statistics office said that whereas exports continued to be strong, consumer spending and construction activity were notably weak. The slowdown in Germany, the euro zone's largest economy, brought the growth figure for the whole euro area down to 0.2% in the second quarter, compared with 0.8% in the first quarter. The disappointing news on Germany came a few days after new figures showed France's economy flatlining in the second quarter.
questions.question: Low consumer spending contributes to:
questions.explanation: Answer (D) is the correct answer as nowhere in the text does it say to what the low consumer spending contributes.

questions.passage: The medial temporal lobes—there's one on each side of the brain—include an arch-shaped structure called the hippocampus and several adjacent regions that together perform the magical feat of turning our perceptions into long-term memories. The memories aren't actually stored in the hippocampus—they reside elsewhere, in the brain's corrugated outer layers, the neocortex—but the hippocampal area is the part of the brain that makes them stick.
questions.question: Where are memories stored?
choices: Both in the hippocampus and neocortex
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (B).

According to the passage: "The memories aren't actually stored in the hippocampus—they reside elsewhere, in the brain's corrugated outer layers, the neocortex."

questions.passage: Pay-television is now under threat, especially in America. Prices have been driven so high at a time of economic malaise that many people simply cannot afford it. Disruptive, deep-pocketed firms like Amazon and Netflix lurk, whispering promises of internet-delivered films and television shows for little or no money. Whether the lure of such alternatives or poverty is what is causing people to cancel their subscriptions is not clear. But the proportion of Americans who pay for TV is falling.
questions.question: How many possible explanations are offered for pay - TV's fall?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is (C).

The passage offers two explanations for the decline of pay-TV: the rise of internet-delivered films and television firms such as Netflix and Amazon, and the high rate of subscriptions.
